theme: The Levite’s concubine; civil war, “no king in Israel”
readingInstruction: Read Judges 19:1-21:25. This is the most disturbing section of the Bible, and it is meant to be. Read it carefully and prayerfully. Do not rush. The story is not an endorsement of what happens but a portrait of moral collapse. Pay attention to how the story echoes the sin of Sodom and to the closing verse of the book.
settingTheScene: This is the second appendix to Judges, and it shows how far Israel has fallen. A Levite’s concubine is raped and killed in Gibeah, a city of Benjamin, and the Levite sends her body in pieces throughout Israel to summon the tribes. The nation gathers in outrage, and a civil war follows that nearly wipes out the tribe of Benjamin. Then Israel, horrified by its own actions, tries to fix the problem by more violence and deceit. The story has no heroes. At its close, the author repeats his summary of the age: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.” The book of Judges ends in darkness because it needs a king.
observation: A Levite takes a concubine from Bethlehem, who goes back to her father’s house, and the Levite goes to bring her back (19:1-3).
On the return journey, he refuses to lodge in Jebus, a foreign city, and chooses Gibeah, a city of Benjamin (19:11-15).
No one in Gibeah takes them in, until an old man from Ephraim offers hospitality (19:15-21).
Worthless men of the city surround the house and demand the Levite, as at Sodom, and the Levite sends out his concubine (19:22-25).
In the morning, the woman is found dead at the door, and the Levite cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them throughout Israel (19:27-30).
All Israel assembles at Mizpah, and the tribe of Benjamin refuses to hand over the guilty men (20:1-13).
After a bloody civil war in which Israel loses tens of thousands in two defeats, Benjamin is almost destroyed, leaving 600 men (20:14-48).
Israel mourns, “Why has this happened in Israel, that today there should be one tribe lacking?” and then secures wives for the survivors by violence and deceit (21:1-23).
“In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (21:25).
interpretation:
The story is a descent into hell. The introduction is subtle: a Levite and his concubine, and a long trip made reluctantly. The Levite refuses to stay in a foreign city and chooses an Israelite one, assuming his own people will be safer. His assumption is exactly wrong. The scene at Gibeah deliberately echoes Genesis 19, where the men of Sodom demanded to abuse Lot’s guests. The author wants us to see that Gibeah, a city in Israel, has become Sodom. The people of God have taken on the character of the nations.

The horror reaches its peak in the Levite’s act of sending out his concubine. The text tells it without comment, and the lack of comment is the comment. No one comes out well. The Levite is a coward, the old man is willing to sacrifice his own daughter and the concubine, and the men of the city are monsters. Later, the Levite’s account to the tribes is self-serving, leaving out his own role. The narrator’s silence invites us to be shocked. This is what happens when a people live without the restraint of God’s word.

The war that follows is complicated. Israel is right to demand justice, but the way they pursue it is flawed. They ask God, “Shall we go up?” and he says yes, but they lose twice, with great casualties. Only after weeping and fasting before the LORD do they win. The text shows a nation seeking God only in crisis, and acting mostly on emotion. The destruction of Benjamin is nearly complete. Then, in chapter 21, the people suddenly realize that they have nearly erased a tribe. They have sworn not to give their daughters to Benjamin, and they cannot fix it without another sin. They attack Jabesh-gilead and kidnap young women from Shiloh. Each solution produces a new crime. The vows, the violence, and the schemes are all expressions of a nation that has lost its moral compass.

The concluding verse is the book’s thesis: no king, and everyone doing what is right in his own eyes. But note the quiet hope. Gibeah is Saul’s hometown. Bethlehem is mentioned as the home of the Levite, and Bethlehem will be David’s home. The book sets up the contrast between a king who fails and a king who shepherds. And behind both, the reader is meant to long for a king who is truly righteous.

Christians read this story as a call to see the depth of sin and the need for a Savior. If this is what human beings do when left to their own judgment, then law and good intentions are not enough. We need a new heart and a true king. The gospel is not a better idea. It is rescue from a disaster we cannot fix. Only Christ, who was himself handed over to wicked men, can heal what Judges 19-21 reveals.
connection: The scene at Gibeah echoes Genesis 19 (Sodom). The cut body parts recall Saul’s summons in 1 Samuel 11:7. Gibeah was Saul’s hometown (1 Samuel 10:26). The refrain “no king” prepares for 1 Samuel 8. Hosea 9:9 and 10:9 refer to “the days of Gibeah” as a byword for corruption. Jesus, handed over to wicked men, is the true suffering king (Matthew 26-27). Romans 3:10-18 describes the universal reach of sin.
application:
Do not look away from this story. Let it increase your sense of what sin does and what Christ saves us from. Spend time in prayer for those who suffer sexual violence and abuse in our own day. Ask the Lord what you can do to protect the vulnerable, such as supporting a ministry, listening to someone’s story, or speaking up.

Second, ask where “what is right in your own eyes” influences your decisions. Choose a recent decision and check it against Scripture. Was it guided by God’s word or by your own reasoning?

Third, let the story deepen your longing for the true king. Pray, “Come, Lord Jesus,” and mean it.
prayerPrompts: Pray for those who suffer violence and betrayal.
Confess where you do what is right in your own eyes.
Pray for Christ’s reign to be real in your life and in the church.
